The earliest fragments are priestly incantations. In one the Salii calm Leucesius, god of lightning. In one the Arval Brethren calm Mars, god of blight, at seed time. Verse fans get a grave survey of five centuries and more.
38595-the-rise-of-the-dutch-kingdom-1795:
Hendrik Willem van Loon wrote a short history of the Netherlands from 1795 to 1813, printed in 1915. He tells how a foreign enemy seized his homeland in the early nineteenth century, and how the land won its freedom again. He dedicated the book to five Belgian soldiers who saved his life near Waerloos.

Chapters trace the last days of the old order, the revolution, and the cost of revolt. They follow national assemblies, coups, and three constitutions at work. Later chapters cover Schimmelpenninck, King Louis of Holland, the liberation, and the restoration under William the First. A closing section compares the four constitutions of Holland. The book gives readers a fast, plain account of how the modern Dutch kingdom took shape.
38861-my-lords-of-strogue-vol-1-of-3-a-c:
My Lords of Strogue, volume one, by Lewis Wingfield, was published in London in 1879. Its subtitle calls it a chronicle of Ireland, from the Convention to the Union. The tale runs to three volumes. A hymn to the God of Peace stands at the front. Wingfield gives the book to a friend named only by initials, in memory of close friendship. Chapter one is called Mirage. It opens in Dublin on November 9, 1783, in a delirium of triumph.

Joy bells rang and green and orange silk hung from every balcony. Citizens in military garb clasped hands in the street. Ireland, the narrator says, had shaken off England's yoke and was free at last. Carriages and troops choked the narrow streets. From that bright day the chronicle unwinds toward the Union.
38862-my-lords-of-strogue-vol-2-of-3-a-c:
My Lords of Strogue, volume two of a chronicle of Ireland from the Convention to the Union, by the Honourable Lewis Wingfield, was published by Richard Bentley and Son in 1879. Wingfield also wrote Lady Grizel. The three volumes tell Ireland's road from the volunteer Convention to the Act of Union. Battle songs stand at the head of the volume.

This volume opens on a night at Crow Street. Doreen, the heiress at its heart, is cooling toward the patriot cause as the decisive moment nears, to the pain of the giant Cassidy. He whispers of pikes and of work done in the night by Phil and Biddy. Chapters follow on Doreen's plans, a duel, and the rising of the tempest. Mr Curran leaves parliament, and the Latin cry of woe to the conquered names the last chapter.
38863-my-lords-of-strogue-vol-3-of-3-a-c:
Lewis Wingfield wrote My Lords of Strogue, a chronicle of Ireland from the Convention to the Union, published by Richard Bentley and Son in London in 1879. This file holds the third of three volumes. Wingfield had earlier written Lady Grizel. The tale closes in the tense years before the Act of Union joined Ireland to Great Britain.

The final volume opens in Dublin, where citizens wait in apprehension and suspense. Lords and Commons, Wingfield writes, suffer the agonies of an evil conscience over the coming settlement. Chapters carry titles of sacrifice and doom: The Shambles, The Altar of Moloch, and Moiley's Last Meal. A list of works consulted follows the tale. The novel dresses high politics in melodrama, with Ireland's fate as its true subject.
38903-the-business-of-mining-a-brief-non:
Arthur J Hoskin wrote The Business of Mining, issued at Philadelphia and London in 1912. The full title calls it a brief, plain account of the rules for profit in mine work. Hoskin was a mining engineer and past professor at the Colorado School of Mines. Sixteen full page pictures and one chart aid the text.

Early chapters ask what a mine is and what mining is. The age of mining and its place in trade follow. Finding mines, claims, and placer work get chapters in turn. Open mining and the checks to make before a mine is opened fill the middle. A front print shows the Utah Copper open pit at Bingham. The book suits new investors and mine men who want plain rules.
39588-the-human-slaughter-house-scenes-f:
Wilhelm Lamszus, a German schoolteacher, wrote this vision of the next war in 1913. Oakley Williams turned it into English, and Alfred Noyes wrote the opening words. Stokes printed The Human Slaughter-House at New York in the year before the guns.

Scenes from the War that is Sure to Come: the subtitle is the whole book in one line. The first note grants its weight: few books of its size — a hundred and eleven pages in the German — have struck so hard. Lamszus had drilled with the colours and seen the new arms. He shows what machine guns, great shells, and gas would do to flesh. We Poor Dead, his epilogue is named. A year later the dead spoke in earnest.
39791-farm-mechanics-machinery-and-its-u:
Herbert Shearer teaches Farm Mechanics, on machinery and its use to save hand labor on the farm, printed at Chicago with copyright in 1918. Drake made the book, with three hundred drawings by the author. Shearer was an agriculturist and had writ a book on farm buildings.

The full title maps the ground. It takes in tools, shop work, driving and driven machines, and farm waterworks. It takes in the care and repair of farm implements as well. The first chapter treats the farm shop, with tools for work in wood and iron. Farm readers get a thick, plain guide to the age when machines took the place of hands.
40372-the-secret-of-the-silver-car-furth:
The Secret of the Silver Car is a crime novel by Wyndham Martyn. Moffat, Yard issued it in New York in 1920. It gives further adventures of Anthony Trent. Trent is a master criminal of a polished kind. The author dedicates the book to his daughters. He jokes about their taste for a thief's career. A puzzling passenger opens the tale. A man dashes past the second officer on a liner.

The man leaps ten feet down to the pier. The great ship cannot pause for him. Talk of the jump fills the smoking room later. A man in the dark and a lady interrupt follow. Count Temesvar and the greater game come later. Anthony plays his hand near the close. Martyn's Trent tales blend crime with high society.
40541-brother-against-brother-or-the-tom:
Brother Against Brother, or The Tompkins Mystery, is a novel of the American Civil War by John Musick. It calls itself a story of the Great American Rebellion. The book came out in New York in 1887 as number 28 of the Fireside Series, a monthly line of cheap fiction. Musick is named on the title page as the author of The Banker of Bedford and other tales.

The Fireside Series sold popular novels by writers such as Braddon and Ouida at low prices. This volume mixes a family split by war with a mystery plot, as its double title promises. It is a sample of the cheap novel trade that fed mass reading in the late nineteenth century.
40574-the-ranche-on-the-oxhide-a-story-o:
A story of boys and girls life on the plains was issued in a Boy Scouts of America edition. The front pages list the national council. Woodrow Wilson stands as honorary president, with William Taft and Theodore Roosevelt as honorary vice presidents. Ernest Thompson Seton is chief scout, and Daniel Carter Beard is national scout commissioner. Headquarters stood in the Fifth Avenue Building in New York.

Scout leaders held that the right story could shape a boy as much as camp craft, and they put sound tales into boys' hands by design. The ranche on the Oxhide tells of young life on a plains ranch: cattle, weather, neighbours, and work. Kansas creek country gives the setting. Scouts of the age read the West through such approved pages, with the movement's blessing stamped at the front.
41105-the-secret-of-charlotte-bronte-fol:
The Secret of Charlotte Bronte is a biographical study by Frederika Macdonald. Jack published it in London and Edinburgh in 1914. Reminiscences of the real Monsieur and Madame Heger follow the study. A portrait by Richmond fronts the volume. Plato's words on love from Diotima stand as an epigraph. Macdonald also wrote The Iliad of the East and lives of Rousseau themes. Her subject is the Brussels episode of Bronte's life. The Hegers ran the school where Charlotte taught and studied.

Her attachment to Monsieur Heger is the secret of the title. Macdonald claims knowledge of the real couple behind the fiction. Villette turned that Brussels world into a famous novel. The reminiscences promise the persons behind Lucy Snowe's story. The book is an early attempt to document Bronte's love. It rests on the author's own Brussels connections and inquiries.
41252-the-assault-germany-before-the-out:
The Assault is a personal narrative of the First World War by Frederic William Wile, published in Indianapolis by Bobbs-Merrill in 1916. Wile had written Men Around the Kaiser. He dedicates the book to Ambassador Gerard and his wife, calling them life-savers, in gratitude. Photographs and copies of documents and cartoons illustrate the text.

The contents are staged like a play. A curtain raiser and a first act open the account of Germany before the outbreak. The plot develops under its stage managers, slow music plays, and the climax brings war itself. Then come the Americans, the fourth of August, and a last farewell. The second half turns to England in war-time: complacency ruling the waves, the helmsmen, the general, the admiral, and the king. Wile writes as an American witness caught between two worlds at war.
41480-christmas-evans-the-preacher-of-wi:
Christmas Evans, the preacher of wild Wales, is a biography by Paxton Hood, shown here in its third edition, issued at London in 1888. Its full title promises the man, his country, his times, and his fellows. Hood had written on the throne of eloquence and on Robert Hall. He inscribes the book to a Brighton minister in a warm letter at the front.

No man living, he writes, could so fitly receive this attempt at the life and labours of Evans. That minister's revered father and Evans were taken into church fellowship on the same evening, he recalls. Within a week they preached their first sermons from the same desk. Then their ways parted, Evans joining himself with the Baptists. From such roots grew the one eyed Welsh preacher whose voice ruled chapels for miles.
41657-to-geyserland-union-pacific-oregon:
Colborn wrote the words and Haynes took the photos for a rail guide dated 1910 to Yellowstone National Park. The Union Pacific and Oregon Short Line roads bring trains from east and west to the park gate. From there, four horse coaches of the stage firm carry guests through the park on set routes.

Hot pools, tall spouts of boiling water, and falls fill the lush prose of the first pages. Elk, deer, buffalo, and bear roam the wilds, and tall pines stand in deep woods. Routes from Kansas City, Omaha, Denver, and Cheyenne are laid out, with notes on bridges, farms, and towns on the way.
41687-how-france-built-her-cathedrals-a-:
How France Built Her Cathedrals is a study of Gothic church craft by Elizabeth OReilly. The book treats the church boom of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Drawings dress the text, and the work came out in nineteen twenty one. The author held rank in a French group for the study of old works.

The first part asks what Gothic craft is and where it grew from. Old basilica forms, bent by rite and by fear in dark years, start the tale. A great abbey house is named the civil force that lit the new age. Shire schools of the old round arch style are traced town by town. Stone saints and glass tales then fill the bulk of the long study.
41707-the-development-of-metaphysics-in-:
The Development of Metaphysics in Persia, a contribution to the history of Muslim philosophy by Muhammad Iqbal, was printed by Luzac in London in 1908. Iqbal dedicates the book to his teacher Arnold, calling it the first fruit of ten years of training. The introduction opens on a national trait: the most remarkable feature of the Persian character, Iqbal writes, is a love of metaphysical speculation.

Yet no Persian system matches Kapila or Kant for completeness. The Persian mind, he argues, is impatient of detail and satisfied with bare universality, while the subtler Brahman dissects experience after experience. Persian depths therefore surface mostly in disconnected verses, the ghazal, which reveal the subtlety of the artistic soul without reviewing the whole garden of thought.
41749-practical-graining-with-descriptio:
William Wall, who bills himself Grainer to the Trade, published Practical Graining at Philadelphia in 1891, with forty-seven coloured plates. The book teaches painters to imitate, in paint, the woods used in interior finishing.

Early chapters cover groundworks, mixing graining colours, and the simpler woods, then quartered oak, ash, and Hungarian ash. Chestnut, bird's-eye and curly maple, satinwood, pollard oak, and cherry follow, then black walnut, mahogany, rosewood, cypress, and hard pine. Wall names the colours for each wood and the handling: wiping the hearts, putting in lights and shades, stippling, and blending. Later chapters treat varnishing, the tools of the trade from combs to badger blenders, patent graining machines, and the imitation of carved work.
42364-faux-s-memorable-days-in-america-1:
Thwaites reprints two English travellers in Early Western Travels, volume 12, printed at Cleveland in 1905. The Arthur Clark Company made the book. The volume holds part two of Faux's Memorable Days in America, and Welby's Visit to North America. Both journeys date to 1819 and 1820.

Faux's journal of a tour to the United States runs here from January 1 to July 21, 1820. Welby's visit takes in the English settlements in Illinois, with a winter residence at Philadelphia. Its stated purpose is plain: to ascertain the actual prospects of the emigrating agriculturist, mechanic, and commercial speculator. Welby's own dedication and preface stand in front of his text. The voyage, ship cookery, and the situation of a passenger on board open his account.
42855-assassination-of-lincoln-a-history:
Harris wrote the Assassination of Lincoln, a history of the great conspiracy. The American Citizen Company at Boston holds the entry from 1892. Harris was a brigadier-general and a member of the commission. That commission tried the conspirators by military process, the title says. A review of the trial of John Surratt stands in the same volume.

Harris opens by explaining his title's key term with care. Great conspiracy here does not mean the whole rebellion, as in Logan's book. It names only the plot that ended in the murder of the President. The trial held importance for the whole civilized world, he holds. His seat on the commission gave him the record from inside. The book gives the plot, the hunt, and the trials in an officer's order.
43113-a-blind-esperantist-s-trip-to-finl:
W Percy Merrick wrote A Blind Esperantist's Trip to Finland and Sweden, printed with the help of the Hastings Esperanto Group. The journey took him to the Fourteenth International Esperanto Congress. On Thursday, August 3, Merrick and his wife left Hull on the Arcturus. Some fifty other Esperantists sailed with them. John Merchant, president of the British Esperanto Association, and Warden, its ex-president, were of the party.

The sea stayed smooth till Saturday, and the party ate and joked in holiday mood. The ship's company were Finns, and only the captain and purser spoke English. The waitresses laughed only once, when a lurch shot a whole table's crockery to the floor. Meals ran in the Finnish manner: breakfast at nine, lunch at twelve, dinner at six. Cold fish, ham, tongue, and hard-bread opened every sitting.
43323-hints-on-cheese-making-for-the-dai:
Hints on Cheese-Making, for the Dairyman, the Factoryman, and the Manufacturer, is a practical treatise by Thomas Curtis. It was printed at Utica, New York, in 1870. The pages first appeared as a series of articles in the Utica Morning and Weekly Herald during the past season. Curtis claims for them a modest place: not a full exhaustion of the questions, but the most practical treatise on cheese-making yet to appear.

He would not check honest criticism, he says, but encourage it. Nor would he have any reader adopt his suggestions if he thinks his own are better. He urges each man to observe closely, experiment thoroughly, and be guided by his own experience. Beginners, he believes, will glean valuable help from the pages, but should accept nothing as conclusive. There is much still to be discovered about cheese-making.
43397-the-comic-english-grammar-a-new-an:
The Comic English Grammar, a new and facetious introduction to the English tongue, came out at London from the press of Richard Bentley in 1840. Its unnamed author had also written The Comic Latin Grammar. Upwards of fifty characteristic pictures by J Leech enliven the book. The dedication honors George Robins in the style of a sale bill. It ends with the bard's words: take him for all in all, we ne'er shall see his like again.

The author's preface wishes his own preface to be like a donkey's gallop, both short and sweet. The joke of the book is to teach the rules of grammar in a laughing way, with mock praise and absurd cases doing the work of lists. Such comic schoolbooks were a fad, and Leech's drawings helped this one outlive its fellows.
43435-shakespeare-as-a-dramatic-artist-a:
Richard G Moulton argues that Shakespeare was a master craftsman, not a careless genius, in a study issued at Oxford in 1885. The Clarendon Press published it. Moulton lectured in literature for the university extension.

His preface names the target plainly. Many readers grant Shakespeare deep knowledge of human nature. Yet they treat him as loose in the craft of drama, too great to need its rules. Moulton fights that view with close studies of single strokes of art. The later chapters go further. They set out dramatic criticism as a regular inductive science. Moulton helped bring great books to working audiences across Britain and America. This early work shows his method whole: read closely, name the device, and prove the design.
43540-letters-from-palestine-written-dur:
Letters From Palestine, by Paxton, records a residence there in the years 1836, 1837, and 1838. Charles Tilt printed the book in London in 1839. The letters are written home as the stay unfolds, place by place.

The first letter is dated at Beyroot on June 18, 1836. Paxton had spent a day at Cyprus in talk with the missionaries there, then sailed with a fine wind. Fog hid the coast at dawn, but the captain called him up as Mount Lebanon showed through. Snow lay on the high parts in patches, bright in the broken cloud. Paxton writes of the power of association: raised on the Bible, he greets the land of its scenes with thanks for his parents' teaching. The letters mix travel notes with a missionary's eye.
44016-the-white-spark-a-new-book-giving-:
The White Spark announces itself as a new book giving out a new philosophy and the mysteries of the universe. Its synopsis names it the handbook of the millennium and the new dispensation. The white spark, or vacuum cell in nature, is in its teaching the right hand of God.

That one principle, the book claims, is the cause and parent of electricity, combustion, radium, snowflakes, flowers, and even life itself. The system promises the road to health, the cause and cure of disease, and the truth about what it calls the germ humbug, drug treatments, serums, and antitoxins. Farmers learn that the nitrogen of the air is only a dust of quartz rocks, and that clover root nodules do not draw nitrogen from the air. The volume is a fringe cosmology, certain of everything and answerable to no laboratory.
44132-tom-strong-lincoln-s-scout-a-story:
Alfred Bishop Mason wrote Tom Strong, Lincoln’s Scout, a boys’ tale of the Civil War. Henry Holt and Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred nineteen. Theodore Roosevelt let Mason give the book to him in his name. His short note from Oyster Bay stands at the front pages.

Tom Strong first meets John Brown on a dark Maryland road. The Harper’s Ferry raid and fight open the boy’s war years. Kit Carson and his lawyer, young Abe Lincoln, share one part. Bull Run, Stonewall Jackson, and McClellan mark the next span. Tom wins a lieutenant’s rank and fights at sea in tale form. He steals a locomotive deep in the foe’s own lines at night. Booth hunts him while he bears Grant’s dispatches west in haste. Lincoln saves a young soldier’s life in a late kind scene.
44381-a-dialogue-in-hades-a-parallel-of-:
A Dialogue in Hades is a military pamphlet attributed to the Chevalier Johnstone. The Literary and Historical Society of Quebec published this reprint in 1887. Its subtitle calls it a parallel of military errors. The errors are those of the French and English armies in Canada in 1759.

The original manuscript rests in the French war archives at Paris. A copy, taken with French permission in 1855, lies in Canada. The work is supposed to have been written about the year 1765. Johnstone was a Scottish Jacobite who fled to France after Culloden. The French king gave him and other Scots commissions in his armies. He sailed in 1748 as an ensign with troops bound for Cape Breton. In the campaign of 1759 he served two famous commanders in turn.
44459-lee-and-longstreet-at-high-tide-ge:
Lee and Longstreet at High Tide is a Civil War history by Helen Longstreet, published by the author at Gainesville, Georgia, in 1904. A portrait of James Longstreet, lieutenant-general, fronts the book. Its subtitle promises Gettysburg in the light of the official records. Facsimiles of letters stand among its illustrations.

The dedication is the author's own. She gives the book to Longstreet at Gettysburg, from her who since childhood has held his heroic deeds, as soldier and citizen, among the priceless inheritances of the great republic. Advance chapters went to the press early in December. By the time the book appeared, the warrior slept serenely, undisturbed by earthly contentions. Helen Longstreet, the general's widow, wrote to defend his conduct on the second day at Gettysburg against a generation of critics. Her book is a widow's brief built on the official record.
44802-the-comic-english-grammar-a-new-an:
Percival Leigh wrote the Comic English Grammar, a facetious introduction. Leech embellished it with forty-five drawings and more in 1845. A preliminary discourse states the author's reasons for producing it. To advance mankind by promoting education is the first object named. Ameliorating the conversation of the masses stands second in its list.

Cultivating taste and diffusing refinement complete its stated aims. Few ears are so obtuse as not to be annoyed, it opens. Violations of grammar assail us in the streets daily, it complains. That 'ere omnibus and where have you been stand as horrors. Cartmen cry strange words to their horses in the same pages. Enormities are perpetrated in spite of many grammars already out. That fact suffices to justify one more grammar, it argues. Leigh teaches the parts of speech with a laugh attached.
44883-the-drama-of-love-and-death-a-stud:
The Drama of Love and Death is a study of human evolution and transfiguration by Edward Carpenter, printed at New York and London in 1912. Mitchell Kennerley issued it. Sixteen chapters and an appendix fill the book. A poem, The Delphian Sibyl overlooking the Earth, stands before the introduction.

The chapters begin with the beginnings of love and love as an art. Then Carpenter turns to dying: the art of dying and the passage of death. An after-death state, the underlying self, and survival of the self take their turns. Notes treat consciousness in the body and mediumistic trance. The closing chapters treat reincarnation, the divine soul, and the return journey.
45051-william-clayton-s-journal-a-daily-:
William Clayton's Journal is the daily record of the journey of the original company of Mormon pioneers from Nauvoo, Illinois, to the valley of the Great Salt Lake. The journal was published in 1921 by the Clayton Family Association, with a biographical introduction. Clayton, born in Lancashire in 1814, was clerk of the pioneer company.

The introduction traces his family from a follower of William the Conqueror who received the manor of Clayton after Hastings. Clayton heard the Mormon gospel in England from Heber Kimball and Orson Hyde, was slow to convert, and emigrated in 1840, becoming a trusted man at Nauvoo. His parents and siblings followed; his mother died at Nauvoo and a brother at Winter Quarters. The journal itself is the day-by-day account of the 1847 trek west, kept by the man appointed to record it, and long valued as a primary source on the trail.
45773-a-proclamation-declaring-his-maies:
The King's proclamation of 1621, printed at London by Bonham Norton and John Bill, declares his pleasure in dissolving the present convention of Parliament. The spelling and capitals of the original printing are kept. The King first asserts that assembling, continuing, and dissolving Parliaments belongs to the Crown alone. He then says that, by his custom, he will acquaint his subjects with the reasons for this public resolution.

The proclamation recalls that this Parliament, begun in January, was called to make good laws and to settle peace and religion in a distracted Christendom. Supply for the treasury was the needful means to those ends. The King insists he meant this to be the happiest Parliament of his time. The blame for its failure is laid on the impediments that arose within it.
46329-the-swamp-doctor-s-adventures-in-t:
The Swamp Doctor's Adventures in the South West is a book of humorous sketches by John Robb, writing as Madison Tensas. Darley drew the pictures, and the book appeared in 1858. It gathers the whole of The Louisiana Swamp Doctor with streaks of squatter life and far western scenes. Forty two sketches describe incidents of the old southwest.

Robb inscribes the volume to two true and fast friends in Madison Parish, Louisiana. The first sketch sets the city physician against the swamp doctor. The city man has all the appliances of refined life around him, and help in critical cases. The swamp doctor rides obscure bridle paths and unbridged streams, through deadened forests where the woodman's axe rings. His patients are young settlers in a country still near its primitive state. These sketches, full of dialect and tall talk, stand among the classics of old southwestern humour.
46354-the-english-village-community-exam:
The English Village Community, a work of history by Frederic Seebohm, studies the old English village in its ties to the manorial and tribal systems. A second thread is the common or open field system of farming. The front matter lists Seebohm's other works, among them The Oxford Reformers. This text keeps the book's Old English letters and marks, with notes on how they are rendered.

Seebohm reads charters, laws, and field patterns as one record. His case is that the village community of the middle ages grew from older tribal roots. Open fields worked in common, he argues, were not a late device but a survival. The book shaped all later study of the English village and its fields.
46514-our-edible-toadstools-and-mushroom:
Hamilton Gibson wrote Our Edible Toadstools and Mushrooms, for Harper at New York in 1895. Thirty colored plates and fifty-seven other pictures, all by Gibson, fill the book. It selects thirty native food varieties for the table. Each is easily known by its marked traits, the title promises. Simple rules for telling the poisonous kinds stand beside the good ones.

A plate of the deadly amanita fronts the warning side of the work. The dedication points readers to that chapter with the author's solicitude. Forewarned is forearmed, the old saying runs at the head of the page. Gerarde's words on those who hunger after mushrooms stand quoted there too. The book began as a magazine article, then grew by popular call. Gibson teaches the hunter to gather dinner and shun death in the same woods.
4704-nomads-of-the-north-a-story-of-roma:
James Oliver Curwood opens Nomads of the North in late March, at the dying out of the Eagle Moon. Neewa the black bear cub gets his first real look at the world. His mother Noozak, old and rheumatic, slept four months that winter instead of three. Neewa, born while she slept, was over two months old, not six weeks, when they left the den. Noozak chose a cavern at a high, barren ridge crest, and Neewa first looked down into a valley.

Coming out of darkness into sunlight, Neewa was blinded for a time, hearing, smelling, and feeling many things before he could see. From that den begins a story of romance and adventure under open stars, following bear and humans through northern seasons. Readers get a warm animal adventure for young and old, with Curwood's love of wild life, and a cub's eye view of a hard, beautiful world.
47219-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appletons' Popular Science Monthly for May 1900 opens volume 57 of the magazine, edited by Cattell and published in New York by McClure, Phillips. The contents list is a cross-section of science at the century's turn, from astronomy to zoology.

The lead article treats the coming total eclipse of the sun, set for May 28, 1900. Bigelow of the Weather Bureau explains the luck of it: the shadow track crosses the Southern States, where thousands can reach it cheaply. Other pieces ask which is the most expensive city in the world. The birds of the Adirondacks, the structure of blind fishes, and a hundred years of chemistry fill the middle. The fate of the Beagle, Darwin's ship, closes the list. Monthly readers got the laboratory and the field in one cover.
47380-recollections-of-thirty-nine-years:
Sir Charles Alexander Gordon wrote Recollections of Thirty nine Years in the Army, issued in London by Swan Sonnenschein and Company in eighteen ninety eight. Gordon was a surgeon general. A photo portrait by Mr A Bassano faces the title page. He inscribed the narrative to his wife and children. A line from Othello heads the book, on battles, sieges, and fortunes.

Chapters run from eighteen forty one, when Gordon was gazetted to the Buffs and reached India. The Gwalior campaign and the battle of Maharajpore fill early chapters. The Gold Coast of Africa in eighteen forty seven and forty eight follows. The Indian Mutiny of eighteen fifty seven and fifty eight fills the centre. The expedition to China and the Siege of Paris close the tale. Army doctors get a long, full service memoir.
47462-castara-the-third-edition-of-1640-:
Castara is a book of poems by William Habington, and this text prints the third edition of 1640. Edward Arber edited it for his English Reprints series in 1895. Arber collated the 1640 text with the earlier editions of 1634 and 1635. His introduction and bibliography, with first lines, show the growth of the work.

The first part holds a prose character of a mistress and fifty-seven poems, chiefly on love and courtship. The second part gives a character of a wife and fifty poems on wedded happiness. A character of a friend and eight elegies follow. Habington's poems to his wife, under the name Castara, are a rare song of married love in English verse.
47697-odette-s-marriage-a-novel-from-the:
Odette's Marriage, a novel from the French of Albert Delpit, came to Chicago in a fifth edition in 1882. Emily Prescott translated the tale from the Revue des Deux Mondes. The book had first been entered for copyright in 1880.

Odette rides slowly up the sandy avenue of a country house and draws rein at the steps. Madame Descoutures leans over the balustrade and calls her up for a talk before she goes in. Odette's beauty is set out at length: a willow grace, a clear skin flushed by the ride, and great dark eyes. The chapters name Laviguerie, Paul Frager, and Germaine, then the marriage itself. A wedding journey, a passion, scandal, and a discovery drive the tale toward a home secret and exposure.
48124-bob-dexter-and-the-storm-mountain-:
Willard Baker sets a boy sleuth climbing in Bob Dexter and the Storm Mountain Mystery, or the secret of the log cabin, printed in New York with copyright in 1925. Cupples and Leon made the book. Baker had writ two Bob Dexter mysteries before it, and the Boy Ranchers series besides. A frontispiece shows the party reaching an island with the maps and papers.

Twenty one chapters of clues follow. The man with the box leads, then the log cabin and startling news. A wooden leg, a mysterious robbery, and strange marks build the case. The key experiment and Jolly Bill's tale fill the mid run. On the trail, sailor's knots, and monkey land vary the hunt. A night pursuit and a singer in the dark raise the stakes. The man with the hook and the last chord close in on new suspicions.
48575-the-century-of-inventions-of-the-m:
The Century of Inventions of the Marquis of Worcester reprints a famed little book of the sixteen hundreds. The marquis listed a hundred inventions in short, riddling hints. A quote at the front urges every mechanic to attend to it. Many of its contrivances seemed most unlikely, the editor notes, yet some of the hardest have been made to answer all the marquis said of them.

Granger's history is quoted for a bold claim: Savery likely took from the marquis the hint of the steam engine for raising water by fire. That one invention, it says, would entitle the author to immortal fame. The editor presents the book as a link in the history of the steam engine. Its merits, he writes, were seen early by men of science. The reprint, with its notes, helped rescue a neglected work. Worcester's century remains a puzzle book of early engineering dreams.
49292-camping-in-the-canadian-rockies-an:
Walter Dwight Wilcox wrote Camping in the Canadian Rockies, published by Putnam's Sons in New York and London in 1896. The book carries twenty-five full-page photogravures and many smaller pictures, all from photographs by the author. Mount Assiniboine fronts the volume.

Wilcox describes camp life in the wilder parts of the Canadian Rockies, and the country around Banff, Lake Louise, and Glacier. A sketch of the early explorations closes the account. In his preface he praises the region's mix of mountain, lake, and forest scenery and its fine summer climate. Over four years he made camping trips into remote valleys and climbed a number of peaks, camera always at hand. The book helped introduce American and British travelers to a range then newly opened by the railway.
49664-gideon-bands-for-work-within-the-r:
Gideon Bands For Work Within The Race And For Work Without It is a sermon to Black Americans by Francis J Grimke, pastor of the Fifteenth Street Presbyterian Church in Washington. He delivered it on Sunday, March the 2nd, 1913, and it was printed by R L Pendleton of Washington. The text is Judges 7:1-7, where God cuts Gideon's army from tens of thousands down to the three hundred men who lapped water like dogs.

Grimke takes that winnowing as his theme. The call, he says, rings out like a want ad: Wanted, men for Gideon's band. A race's progress, on his telling, depends not on numbers but on a small company of tested people willing to work within the race and for it beyond.
49858-studies-on-homer-and-the-homeric-a:
Studies on Homer and the Homeric Age, volume two, by the Right Honourable W E Gladstone, was printed at the University Press, Oxford, in 1858. Gladstone was then member of parliament for the university. The volume bears its own title: Olympus, or the Religion of the Homeric Age. A line of Horace stands as motto.

Gladstone holds that Homer's system of gods is a mixed thing, part tradition and part invention. Its incongruities, he argues, point to diversity of sources. He reads it as a true theology corrupted over time, not a growth from nature worship alone. Leading traditions of Scripture, on the Godhead, a Redeemer, and an Evil One, are set beside their defaced counterparts in Homer. The downward course of the idea of God fills the first section.
4991-the-pony-rider-boys-in-new-mexico-o:
Four boys calling themselves the Pony Rider Boys ride into New Mexico in this western adventure, and even strangers in a rail car have heard of their lively stunts. Two men whisper about the boys behind them, one snoring in the seat, wondering whether kids out for a holiday could really be as tough as report says.

The answer comes on plains and mountains, as the boys chase the end of the silver trail through scrapes and dangers. The catalog record leaves the author unnamed. Readers get a boys' western of horses, humor, and teamwork, where youth itself becomes a kind of courage on the trail.
50058-marion-harland-s-complete-etiquett:
Marion Harland's Complete Etiquette is a guide to manners by Harland and Virginia Van de Water. Bobbs-Merrill issued the revised edition at Indianapolis. Copyrights run from 1905 to 1914. Its subtitle calls it a young people's guide to every social occasion. The contents list runs to more than forty chapters. Invitations and cards open the instruction. Letter writing and introductions follow.

Weddings at home and in church get chapters of their own. The dinner party and the debutante come next. Chaperons, dress, and gifts are treated in turn. Bachelor hospitality and hotel life widen the range. Mourning, travel, and sport each have their rules. Mistress and maid close the social ladder. Such books taught the forms of a strict age. They promised ease to the young and unsure.
50436-protestantism-and-catholicity-comp:
Balmes wrote this comparison of Protestantism and Catholicity in Europe. Murphy printed the second edition in Baltimore in 1851. Balmes wrote in Spanish, the work Englished here from French. His preface opens on evils born of modern revolutions shock.

Earth seemed to open under our feet in those shocks, he writes. Man asked what am I, whence do I come, in alarm. Religious questions regained high importance against all expectation then. They rose predominant over society in gigantic form, he contends. Material interests and exact sciences seemed set to stifle those questions for good.
51548-early-greek-philosophy-other-essay:
Friedrich Nietzsche's early essays appear in volume two of his complete works in English, translated by Maximilian A Mügge and edited by Oscar Levy, in 1911. Contents list The Greek State and a fragment on the Greek woman, both from 1871. On music and words and Homer's Contest follow from the same early years.

Philosophy during the tragic age of the Greeks and On Truth and Falsity date to 1873. The translator calls most of these pieces fragments, many meant as prefaces to unwritten books. He finds traces of Nietzsche's later tenets everywhere in them. Slave and master morality and the Superman, he says, are already visible in embryo.
51607-address-delivered-at-the-quarter-c:
Governor John Martin of Kansas gave this address at Topeka on January 29th, 1886. The occasion was the quarter-centennial celebration of the admission of Kansas as a state. The Kansas Publishing House printed the speech the same year, under the title 'The Development of Kansas' for the address itself.

Martin opens with a Greek myth, of Zeus warned that a son would take his place. From the god's cloven head sprang Athena, full-armed and with a war shout. The tale serves as a figure for a state born in struggle, and Martin turns from myth to the growth of Kansas in twenty-five years.
5204-the-inns-and-taverns-of-pickwick-wi:
B. W. Matz's study follows the inns and taverns of Dickens's Pickwick Papers through the coaching age. Chapters visit the Golden Cross at Charing Cross, the Bull at Rochester, the White Hart in the Borough, La Belle Sauvage, the Leather Bottle at Cobham. The Town Arms at Eatanswill appears among many others.

Matz pairs each inn with its scene in the novel and with its later history, using engravings and local records. The book serves both Dickens readers, who want to walk Pickwick's road. Students of old English inns get their share too: how coaching houses lived, changed, and sometimes vanished.
52156-a-history-of-parliamentary-electio:
Joseph Grego wrote this history of parliamentary elections and electioneering in the old days, published in London by Chatto and Windus in 1886. Grego had written lives of the caricaturists Gillray and Rowlandson, and this book leans on the same art. A print on the rights of women stands near the front.

The subtitle states the plan: to show the state of political parties and party warfare at the hustings and in the House of Commons from the Stuarts to Queen Victoria. The pictures come from the original political squibs, lampoons, prints, and caricatures of each age. Candidates address their crowds, and the verses mock both Tories and Whigs for buying votes and praising commonplaces. Readers get British election history told largely in the savage cartoons of the time.
52864-bessbrook-and-its-linen-mills-a-sh:
Bessbrook and Its Linen Mills describes an Irish model temperance town. Ritchie wrote the short narrative. Tweedie published it in London in 1876. Ritchie had written on the religious life of London before it. David Price transcribed this copy from that edition. The town's linen mills anchor its order.

The book opens with a broad social lament. Our times are out of joint, Ritchie writes. The rich grow richer and the poor poorer. Peasants are driven into towns of bad air and bad pay. Talk and associations multiply without curing the rot. Against that background one Irish spot stands out. Silent, steady betterment has worked there for twenty years. The narrative presents Bessbrook as its proof. Temperance is the town's founding rule.
53562-underground-treasures-how-and-wher:
Underground Treasures, by James Orton, was published in 1881. Baird issued this new edition at Philadelphia. Orton had taught natural history at Vassar College. The Andes and the Amazon stands among his books. The subtitle promises a key to all useful minerals in the United States. Chapter one opens on money in the rocks. Great fortunes are missed through ignorance, Orton warns. Valuable minerals go about in disguise. Chapter two teaches the reader to name a specimen. A jack-knife and common sense are the chief tools. Pyrites must be told from gold, quartz from diamond. The key sorts minerals by hardness and colour.

Chapter three lists the useful kinds from agate to zinc. Marks, uses, and localities are given for each. Gems, precious metals, and ores all stand in the list.
53578-the-mausoleum-at-halicarnassus-res:
James Fergusson, a fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects, wrote this short study of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, published by John Murray in London in 1862. The tomb ranked among the seven wonders of the ancient world, and Fergusson aims to rebuild it on paper from remains that had only lately come to light.

Fergusson admits the essay is no full account of the monument, only a gathering of the data that might solve a riddle long puzzling students of classical building. He reviews the old written sources, the surviving fragments, and other tombs used as models, then works through Greek measures, the cymatium, and the pteron. From there he settles the pyramid, the vertical heights, and the placing of sculpture and pedestals. Plates show his restored south east view.
54073-frank-reade-jr-s-submarine-boat-or:
Frank Reade Junior's Submarine Boat, or To the North Pole Under the Ice, is a dime novel from Frank Reade Weekly Magazine, number 2, dated 7 November 1902. It was written under the pen name Noname and sold for five cents. The story opens with two lost explorers crying out in wonder. The Irishman Barney swears the craft before them is the Explorer itself.

Chapter one, The New Invention, reports that Frank Reade Junior of Readestown has brought out a new device, and the news has spread far with great excitement. Frank, son of a noted inventor, came by his talent honestly. Still almost a boy, he holds a place in fame's records that grown men might envy. The submarine boat carries the adventure north under the ice.
54697-the-baita-l-pachchisi-or-the-twent:
The Baital Pachchisi is a translation of the Hindi story cycle known as the twenty-five tales of a sprite, made by John Platts from the text edited by Duncan Forbes. Allen published it in London in 1871. The baital is a vampire-like spirit who hangs from a tree and tells riddling tales to a king who must carry him in silence.

Platts explains his aim in the preface. The translation was made by special request, to meet repeated demands for Forbes's text in English. It is meant to let the student study the original with ease and accuracy, so it keeps as literal as English idiom allows. Notes meet the difficulties head-on. Platts warns that the translation does not replace the grammar. The tales themselves, of the king and the corpse-spirit, are among the oldest story machines in the world.
55190-florida-and-the-game-water-birds-o:
Florida and the Game Water-Birds of the Atlantic Coast and the Lakes of the United States is a sporting book by Robert Barnwell Roosevelt. It was printed at New York in 1884. Roosevelt also wrote The Game-Fish of North America and Superior Fishing. The book adds remarks on breech-loaders and hammerless guns.

In his preface Roosevelt says he first wrote the account of Florida, a sporting country never yet fully described. For the part on the game birds of the waters and coasts he quotes freely from a kindred book of his own. His main purpose is to call sportsmen to the southern peninsula, a paradise for the devotee of rod and gun. Game is vanishing from the home country, he warns: woodcock and grouse are almost wiped out, and ducks grow scarce. Florida, by contrast, still promises a larger bag than the North can give.
55539-korean-tales-being-a-collection-of:
Korean Tales, by Allen, gathers stories translated from Korean folk lore. Putnam's Sons issued the book in New York and London in 1889. Allen served as foreign secretary of legation for Korea, and two opening chapters describe the country.

Those chapters treat the land, its people and government, and the sights in and about the capital. A note explains the national emblem: heaven and earth as male and female, in blue and yellow. Allen says folk at home kept asking why he did not write a book on Korea. He points them first to the large work by Griffis on the hermit kingdom. His own tales include the rabbit legends, an enchanted wine jug, and why cat and dog are enemies. Faithful wives and dutiful daughters close the set.
55585-manual-of-style-governing-composit:
The Government Printing Office in Washington issued this manual of style in 1894. It governs composition and proof reading in that office, prepared under the Public Printer. Abbreviations lead the contents at page eight, and capitalization fills pages nine to sixteen in the list.

Compounding, bill style, court work and journal work get their own sections in the contents. Geographic names, Greek accents and the Greek alphabet stand toward the back of the book. Printers of laws, reports and testimony worked by these rules, and the manual fixed one federal house style for spelling, capitals and figures in American print.
55594-my-opinions-and-betsey-bobbet-s-de:
Marietta Holley wrote this comic book under the name Josiah Allen's Wife, and the American Publishing Company of Hartford issued it by subscription in 1884. Its long title calls it a beacon light to guide women to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. She dedicates it to Josiah, her lawful partner of more than 14 years.

In the preface, Samantha tells how her mind turned to the great subject of women's rights once the farm mortgage was paid and the children were off at school. A voice in her kept saying to write a book and give her views. The talk runs in rich country dialect, and the humor carries a sharp point. Readers get laughs on the surface and a plain case for women's freedom under them.
55776-history-of-the-royal-sappers-and-m:
This first volume tells the story of the Royal Sappers and Miners, the British Army's corps of works and mines. Its span runs to October 1856, as the title states. A plate at the front shows a Soldier Artificer Company in the uniform of 1786.

The artificers were the army's skilled hands: diggers, builders, and miners in one. From such companies grew the corps whose tale this book tells in full. Campaigns across the world called on their picks and spades as much as on muskets. Siege works, roads, and bridges stand in their record. The volume sets the corps's birth and first long age in order for the men who served in it.
57123-kellogg-s-great-crops-of-strawberr:
Kellogg Great Crops of Strawberries and How to Grow Them is a 1922 nursery book. The Kellogg Company of Three Rivers, Michigan, issued it to sell pedigree plants. Its star sort is branded Delicious, the strawberry that satisfies, in the ads. Bank officers of the town vouch for the firm in print up front.

A state nursery inspection certificate backs each shipment of plants, it says. The bank letter calls Kellogg the world largest exclusive strawberry nursery then. Fair dealing and plants true to name are pledged to every buyer. Photos of shortcake, plants, and bank men fill the sales pitch throughout. Growing method, the Kellogg way, is the heart of the book.
57381-diary-kept-by-rifleman-b-c-stubbs-:
The diary kept by Rifleman Stubbs of the second draft sent to the Queen Victoria Rifles in France was printed in Chicago in 1915, with a 1916 copyright. Stubbs, full name Bernard Castle Stubbs, worked for the Union-Castle Line in London and joined the 9th Battalion, London Regiment, in September 1914. Verses by Kipling front the book.

A memoir note says Stubbs volunteered for the first draft to fill gaps in his unit and went straight to the firing line in February. He fought in the famed clash on Hill 60 on the night of April 20-21, under an officer who won a Victoria Cross. A shell wound on June 22 ended his service and his life. The diary keeps his own voice.
57485-index-for-works-of-andrew-barton-b:
David Widger compiled an index with links to the works of Andrew Barton Paterson, the Australian poet known as Banjo. The file is not a tale but a guide: it lists each book of Paterson's verse and tales with its full table of contents. Readers can jump from this index to the work they want.

Volumes listed include The Man from Snowy River and Others, Rio Grande's Last Race, and Saltbush Bill and Other Verses. Story sets such as Three Elephant Power and the novel An Outback Marriage are here too, as are The Old Bush Songs. First lines are given for many poems, so a half recalled verse can be traced to its home in print.
57783-the-legislative-manual-of-the-stat:
The Legislative Manual of the State of Colorado is a reference book put together by Thomas B. Corbett and printed at Denver in 1877, the year after statehood. It joins a short history of the state, the annals of its legislature, a manual of customs, precedents and forms, and rules of parliamentary practice. It also prints the constitutions of the United States and of Colorado.

Corbett speaks first to legislators, but he promises matter of use to lawyers, merchants and the young ripening into public life. The early history is kept brief and plain, he says, because settlement began scant twenty years before and living men could be hurt by partial sketches. The annals took much labour, for the journals were imperfect and many members had left the territory. Biennial editions were planned.
58118-useful-knowledge-volume-3-animals-:
Useful Knowledge, volume 3, treats the animal productions of nature. The Rev William Bingley wrote the familiar account of nature's productions used by man. Baldwin, Cradock, and Joy published this fourth edition in London in 1825. Bingley had earlier written Animal Biography. The three-volume work covers mineral, vegetable, and animal productions. This volume is the animals volume.

Its plates map the animal kingdom in numbered figures. The frontispiece sets heads of quadrupeds on the outline of a great whale's head. Rhinoceros, seal, camel, bison, and hog appear in the first plate. A second plate shows parts of mammiferous animals, from the manis to the horse. Birds fill a third, reptiles and fishes a fourth. Lobster, prawn, crab, and oysters close the fifth. The introduction defines its science plainly. Animals possess organisation, life, sensation, and voluntary motion. Zoology treats their arrangement, structure, habits, instincts, and uses to mankind.
58890-the-mysteries-and-miseries-of-san-:
An unnamed Californian wrote this exposé of San Francisco, printed by Garrett and Company of New York and entered for rights in 1853. The title page vows to show up all the types and famed names, high and low, that had marked the city since its settlement. Hills, harbor, and sun open the scene.

The first chapter is named for alarm, flames, and a ladder, and fire hangs over the young city from the start. Houses of the rich crown the round hills, while the town below teems with new men and new schemes. Gold-rush San Francisco gets a tour of its sins, its fires, and its sharpers, told by a writer who claims to know them all.
59260-history-of-the-royal-sappers-and-m:
Volume two of the History of the Royal Sappers and Miners runs to the name change of the corps. Connolly, a stores chief of the Royal Engineers, wrote the past. A London Longman house brought out this grown print in eighteen fifty seven. The corps tale starts with its form in March of seventeen seventy two. Its name changed to Royal Engineers in October of eighteen fifty six.

Seventeen hue plates of garb and gear dress the two book set. Part heads for eighteen forty eight open with staff posts and a London survey. A watch post on Saint Paul spire and a fight on the survey mark that part. North pole trip prep and coast work by corps men fill more heads. Names of rank and file stand thick in the year heads.
59429-fighting-joe-or-the-fortunes-of-a-:
William Adams, writing as Oliver Optic, wrote Fighting Joe, a story of the Great Rebellion published at Boston by Lee and Shepard. The book first appeared in 1865 and was copyrighted again in 1893. It is the fifth volume of his Army and Navy Stories. A picture shows a scene at the battle of Antietam. Adams dedicated the book to a friend in a formal page.

In his preface Adams makes a point clear. The volume is not a biography of the distinguished soldier whose nickname gives the title. Fighting Joe was the army's name for General Hooker. Adams borrows the name for his hero, a staff officer whose fortunes the story follows through the Civil War. Optic's books taught boys the war as adventure, with battles, camps, and escapes. This one gives a young reader the war from headquarters, where orders are carried and plans succeed or fail.
59851-the-chaldean-magician-an-adventure:
Ernst Eckstein wrote The Chaldean Magician, an adventure in Rome in the reign of the Emperor Diocletian, Englished from the German by Mary Safford and printed in New York in 1886. Eckstein had written Quintus Claudius. The first chapter opens on a cloudless October day in the year 299, drawing to a close. The western sky behind the crest of Mount Janiculum still glows with crimson light.

Below, the people are already moving in a blue dusk. Yellow-red lamps shine, veiled by smoke, from the taverns of the many-gabled Subura. A youth with a white toga over his shoulders turns into the Cyprian Way. His walk is odd: now he rushes forward, now he stops, as if repenting his design. Passing the Baths of Titus, he sees another youth and knows a friend's face in the pale features: Lucius Rutilius, unseen for nearly six weeks.
60773-the-philosophy-of-health-volume-1-:
Southwood Smith wrote a health book that ties body, mind, and long life. Smith was a doctor at the London Fever Hospital. This third form, volume one, came out in London in 1847. The full title says the aim plainly. It seeks the roots of long life and joy in how man is made.

Early chapters sort life in plants, beasts, and man. Later chapters ask how sense, thought, and love give joy. One part weighs how health links to years of life, with facts from Rome and England. Readers get an old but clear plan for care of self. Smith writes in plain terms that a home reader can grasp with ease.
60937-the-philosophy-of-health-volume-2-:
Southwood Smith wrote The Philosophy of Health, an exposition of the physical and mental constitution of man, with a view to human longevity and happiness. Volume two in a third edition was issued in London by C Cox in eighteen forty seven. Smith was physician to the London Fever Hospital, the Eastern Dispensary, and the Jews Hospital. Long chapters treat one bodily function at a time in full detail.

Chapter eight treats respiration in plants and in animals, in water and in air. It traces breathing gear from low to high forms, then treats the windpipe, lungs, and air cells in man. Counts of air and blood used in each breath follow, with changes wrought on each. Chapter nine treats the making of heat in living bodies, in plants and in warm and cold blooded beasts. Victorian health readers got deep, plain science.
6131-wonders-of-creation-a-descriptive-a:
Wonders of Creation gives a popular account of volcanoes and their phenomena, meant for the young in 1872. Its epigraph from Nahum pictures mountains quaking, hills melting, and earth burning at divine presence, while the preface avoids scientific detail and philosophical speculation.

A reading of the pages may so stir youthful curiosity that some, on reaching riper years, will inquire more deeply into volcanic agency, its causes, and modes of operation. Some may even climb nearer active volcanoes and examine phenomena themselves. The book treats fire mountains as marvels meant to wake inquiry.
61398-the-polar-world-a-popular-descript:
Hartwig, a German writer on nature, described the polar world for general readers in a book printed in New York in 1869. He had written The Sea and Its Living Wonders and The Tropical World. Added chapters and one hundred sixty three pictures fill this edition. Alaska and the Innuits get new chapters from another hand.

Hartwig aims to show the main features of the Arctic and Antarctic lands. He tells how the long winter night and brief summer shape plant and animal life. Then he pictures man in that hard climate, both the native who lives there and the bold explorer who probes its secrets. Solid teaching in a lively form is his stated goal.
61572-general-history-of-civilisation-in:
General History of Civilisation in Europe, from the fall of the Roman Empire till the French Revolution, is a course of lectures by Guizot, the French historian and statesman. Chambers issued this edition at Edinburgh in 1848, adding a life of Guizot and his treatise on death punishments. The life runs from his birth in 1787 through his literary works, political career, and exile.

The lectures open with the objects of the course and the nature of civilisation itself. Then come the peculiar features of civilisation in Europe, and the influence of the church. The feudal system, the church from the fifth to the twelfth century, and the rise of the boroughs follow. Crusades, royalty, and the union of the elements of modern society fill the later lectures. Guizot's course made him famous across Europe. This cheap edition carried his grand story of progress to Scottish and English readers.
61659-saddle-sled-and-snowshoe-pioneerin:
John McDougall wrote this memoir of pioneering on the Saskatchewan in the sixties, published at Toronto in 1896. Laughlin drew the plates, and the frontispiece shows the author melting snow to boil his kettle over a fire. Dog trains, sleds and snowshoes carry the work of travel in deep winter.

Chapter one starts at Old Fort Edmonton, with early missionaries on the river. A run down the Saskatchewan by dog-train and camp-fire scenes lead home in the summary. A foraging trip, a hungry camp and a welcome feast follow, with dogs, sleds and a buffalo bull tangled together, and a visit to a Wood Cree camp.
61735-uncle-wiggily-goes-swimming-or-how:
Howard Garis's Uncle Wiggily Goes Swimming, pictured by Lang Campbell, is number eighteen in the Uncle Wiggily picture books from Charles Graham of Newark. Copyrights run from the McClure Newspaper Syndicate's 1919 to Graham's 1924. Each book holds three stories; this one adds Uncle Wiggily Distributes Thanksgiving Cakes and The Bunny Rabbit Gentleman Makes a Kite. The title story opens at the pond, where Bully and Bawly No Tail, the frog boys, dive from the spring board.

Uncle Wiggily, recalling his youth, takes off his coat while Nurse Jane is away and jumps in on the count of three. He sticks head-first in the mud, and the frog boys haul him out by the leg and set him on a raft to rest. The numbered paragraphs and big type suit read-aloud picture-book use. Garis lists seventeen companion volumes on the back page.
61903-the-cable-game-the-adventures-of-a:
Stanley Washburn wrote an account of an American press boat in Turkish waters during the Russian Revolution, published in Boston in 1912. A photograph shows the dispatch boat France at anchor in Odessa harbor. Washburn begins with war's end in Manchuria and a new assignment in Russia. A race across Ceylon, India, and the Suez Canal follows.

At Constantinople the party charters a tug as dispatch bearers. They sail the Black Sea for sixty five hours, shaking dice with death, as a chapter puts it. They land at Odessa on a day set for general massacre and find martial law in force. The run for an uncensored cable drives the tale.
62621-memorials-of-shrewsbury-being-a-co:
Memorials of Shrewsbury is a guide to the town and its environs by Henry Pidgeon, printed by John Eddowes at Shrewsbury in 1837. It carries thirty-six engravings and the town motto, Floreat Salopia. Pidgeon dedicates it to the Reverend William Gorsuch Rowland, for his zealous work in restoring several of the town's churches. His preface says a little manual for the enquiring stranger had long been required.

An ardent attachment to his native place, and the wishes of many friends, induced him to undertake the task. The contents survey preserved in the copy shows its range: Shrewsbury's situation, foundation, and etymology; the town under the Britons; Stephen besieging the castle. It was taken by Llewelyn; royal visits and the Great Parliament follow. The Battle of Shrewsbury, Owen Glendower, and the birth there of Richard and George Plantagenet come in turn.
63033-emanuel-swedenborg-s-investigation:
Martin Ramström of the University of Uppsala wrote this study of Emanuel Swedenborg's work in natural science. It first appeared in the festival book for the 200th year of the Royal Society of Sciences of Uppsala, on November 19, 1910, when Swedenborg's sarcophagus was unveiled in the cathedral. The university press printed it the same year.

Ramström sorts Swedenborg's science into fields. One part covers his work in mathematics, mechanics, and astronomy, then geology, mineralogy, chemistry, physics, and cosmology. A third part treats his studies of the body. The second half asks what ground Swedenborg had for his claims about the brain: its centers for life functions, for sense, and for motion, and his doctrine of localization. A copper plate from Swedenborg's 1734 works serves as frontispiece. Scholars get a careful audit of a thinker's science before his fame as a seer.
63245-white-man-bery-unsartin-nigger-hai:
Adams wrote The Washers and Scrubbers: The Men Who Robbed Them, a pamphlet printed at Washington in 1878. Adams had written The Siege of Washington and Story of a Trooper. A second title names the charge without mercy: the blackest chapter in the history of the Republican Party. Its subject is the Freedmen's Bank.

Two sayings from the days of slavery stand at the head of the text, about white men's uncertain faith and the freedman's want of friends. Adams builds his case on the last report of the commissioners winding up the bankrupt bank. The report, he writes, is one of the most remarkable documents ever given to the American people. It shows the heartlessness of man and the scoundrelism inside the country's politics. The bank had held the hard earnings of the freed people. Historians get Reconstruction's savings scandal argued in anger.
63273-thirty-years-from-home-or-a-voice-:
Samuel Leech's Thirty Years from Home, or a Voice from the Main Deck, is kept in the reprint of 1909 by William Abbatt of New York. It appeared as extra number nine of The Magazine of History. The original came from Tappan & Dennet of Boston in 1843. A frontispiece engraving shows the United States frigate, under Decatur, capturing the British Macedonian.

Leech was six years in the British and American navies. He was captured in the Macedonian herself, afterwards entered the American navy, and was taken again in the brig Syren by the British ship Medway. Letters of recommendation stand before the narrative: Erastus Corning of Albany, writing in December 1842, vouches for twenty years' knowledge of Leech as a man of strict integrity.
6357-snowflakes-and-sunbeams-or-the-youn:
R. M. Ballantyne plunges his reader into arctic winter and the wilderness of North America, introducing the chief persons of his tale. An old fur trader tries to fix his son's flint and finds it harder than expected. A counting room scene follows, and a wolf hunt in the prairies lets Charley astonish his father and break in a new horse. Peter Mactavish turns amateur doctor, Charley tells Kate his views, and Kate grows sagacious.

Spring brings voyageurs, a store, farewell to Kate, and Charley's departure with the brigade as a voyageur. The voyage, encampment, and surprise follow, with sporting beginnings, whisky John caught, and a storm. Ballantyne gives boys a northern life of snow, trade, and hard travel, told with the cheerful detail of a man who knows the country.
65692-progress-and-achievements-of-the-c:
Kelly Miller and Joseph R Gay wrote Progress and Achievements of the Colored People, with rights pages dated nineteen thirteen and nineteen seventeen. Miller was dean at Howard University in Washington. More than one hundred photos of real scenes fill the book.

The subtitle calls the rise of Black Americans the most wondrous advance in the history of nations. Photos show bankers of a national association, a capable office staff, and typesetters at work. Business men of a national league and a fine private library appear. The book serves as a handbook for self-improvement. It looks back at past gains and forward to a triumphant era.
66423-a-concise-practical-treatise-on-ar:
A Concise Practical Treatise on Artificial Fly Fishing for Trout comes from Grey Drake, an artificial fly-fisher of fifty years' experience. Published in London in 1860 at one shilling and sixpence, the handbook aims to start beginners cheaply and with little trouble. Its chapters move through tackle, artificial flies, throwing the fly, tying on a hook, bob-flies, and dibbing.

Grey Drake gives no directions for making rods, lines, or flies. He sends readers to the best tackle shops instead. The rod, he argues, can scarcely be too light and pliable. A single-handed rod of about thirteen or fourteen feet serves him well. A skilled hand, he says, can throw a fly as far as needed with one. He prefers a spring cog-check reel. He also treats tying flies by the riverside, in imitation of the fly on the water, as needless.
67108-hints-on-the-history-and-managemen:
Edward Bevan gave these hints on the honey bee in two lectures. The Hereford Times office printed them in the year 1851. Bevan spoke to a Hereford learned society in winter 1850 to 1851. Praise for the talks led him to print a few copies.

Bevan calls himself a very old man but a young lecturer. This was his first speech to a public assembly ever. The society president call to duty drew him to speak. His theme is the history and care of the honey bee. He throws his mite of learning into the common stock, as the president asked of all.
6714-dave-dashaway-and-his-hydroplane-or:
Roy Rockwood sends Dave Dashaway aloft in a hydroplane for daring adventures over the Great Lakes. The tale opens at an aero meet in Columbus, where a messenger boy stares in wonder at a great prize monoplane in its hangar. The man in charge, one-armed, limping, scarred like a war veteran, takes the telegram for Dave.

From that hangar, Dave flies into contests, rescues, and scrapes over lake and shore, with pluck as his chief fuel. Rockwood keeps the pace fast and the talk boyish. Dave Dashaway and His Hydroplane is a breezy, early aviation book for boys, full of machines, nerve, and lake air.
67353-lynch-law-an-investigation-into-th:
Lynch-Law is a study of the history of lynching in the United States by James Elbert Cutler. Cutler taught economics at Wellesley College and had held posts at Yale. The book came out in 1905 from Longmans, Green, and Company of New York, London, and Bombay. The contents set out a full plan in nine chapters.

The first chapter is a broad opening, and the second traces the rise of the term lynch-law. Early lynch-law stands third, and the years from 1830 to 1860 fourth. The Reconstruction period and a chapter called Lynchings stand next in the list. Lynch-Law and Its Justification, Remedies, and a last chapter close the work. The book is a work of research on a grim part of American life, built as a scholar's account of its roots and growth.
67770-bee-keeping-for-profit-a-new-syste:
Lizzie Cotton of West Gorham, Maine wrote Bee Keeping for Profit, a new system of bee management, in its third edition of 1891. The illustrated book sold for one dollar. Cotton says she kept bees almost from childhood and studied all the works and journals on the subject.

Her preface complains that theory, guess-work, and prejudice confuse beginners and cost them money. Early losses taught her the need of a correct and scientific system. Chapters present her controllable hive, then feeding, boxes for surplus honey, and swarming and hiving. Others treat the bee moth, robbing, queen rearing, and the sources of honey. Wintering, transferring, and Italian bees follow, with monthly duties and a chapter on profits. The book speaks to farm families who kept bees as a business.
68703-constantine-the-great-the-reorgani:
John Firth, once a scholar of Queen's College, Oxford, wrote this life of Constantine the Great. Putnam brought it out in 1905 in the Heroes of the Nations line. Firth had earlier written on Augustus Caesar and turned Pliny's letters into English.

His subject is the emperor who reshaped the Roman world. The subtitle names the twin themes: the remaking of the empire and the triumph of the church. A front plate from the British Museum shows Constantine in profile. Readers get a full life of the ruler whose reign joined state power and the Christian faith in ways that shaped all Europe after him.
68724-an-historical-and-moral-view-of-th:
An Historical and Moral View of the French Revolution is a study by Mary Wollstonecraft. Her full title adds the effect of the revolt on the whole of Europe. The book came out in London in the year seventeen ninety four. A print of the author stands at the front of the first volume.

Her note says the work grew past plan with lore of manners and thought. She aims to trace how the spread of facts shapes the acts of states. Creed fog and bright clear thought clash in her frame of the age. More books were in draft to carry the tale past this first one. The work stands as a first hand plea from a famed rights voice.
68769-a-classical-dictionary-containing-:
J Lempriere compiled this classical dictionary, printed in London by George Routledge and Sons in 1904. The full title promises a copious account of all the proper names mentioned in ancient authors. It adds the value of coins, weights, and measures used among the Greeks and Romans. A chronological table stands with the entries.

In his preface Lempriere says he wished to give the most accurate account he could of each name met in reading the classics. Anecdotes and facts of history are gathered in to draw a picture of ancient times. Students of Greek and Latin books get one volume that ties names to places, persons, and things. Spelling varies in the old style, and notes aid the modern reader.
68812-the-schoolmaster-s-trunk-containin:
The Schoolmaster's Trunk, containing papers on home life in Tweenit, by Diaz, was printed by Osgood at Boston in 1875. A note explains the title: the papers first appeared in Hearth and Home, observations from actual life by a teacher in a country village.

Fifteen chapters of observation follow. The slaves of the rolling pin, a word to the men folks, and concerning common things come first. The sewing circle chapters and a talk in the schoolhouse follow. Chapter one opens on a grievance. Pies again, always pies: five times in ten days, pies have stood in the way of better things. His hostess Fennel, far from well with a large family to cook for, could not leave for a ride because they were out of pies. Her daughter Martha declined a library book, and missed a sunset from the hill, for the same cause.
68864-ramsey-carmick-contract-letter-fro:
A House executive document of the 33rd Congress, printed in February 1855, carrying the Postmaster General's letter on the Ramsey and Carmick mail contract. The letter transmits a conditional contract of March 1853 and all the correspondence about it.

The contract would have extended the New Orleans and Vera Cruz mail line onward from Vera Cruz via Acapulco to San Francisco, giving a weekly mail between the Atlantic and Pacific. The Postmaster General objected that a proposed schedule change would frustrate that aim and pay the Pacific Mail company twice for one service. He notes the contractors admitted, nine months on, that they were not ready to perform. Readers get a small paper trail of Gold Rush-era mail politics.
69458-uncle-wiggily-and-mother-goose-com:
Howard Garis wrote Uncle Wiggily and Mother Goose, published in New York by Fenno in 1916. The book holds fifty-two stories, one for each week in the year. Edward Bloomfield drew the pictures. It stands complete in two parts.

Garis had already filled shelves with tales of the old rabbit. Uncle Wiggily Longears and his seashore and country trips came first. Here the rabbit meets the folk of the nursery rhymes. The opening tells where the old rabbit gentleman lives. His home is a hollow-stump bungalow in the woods. Nurse Jane Fuzzy Wuzzy, a muskrat lady, keeps house for him. Weekly stories carry young readers through a whole year of visits.
70649-catalogue-of-valuable-paintings-an:
The American Art Association issued a sale catalogue at New York in 1907 for a set of paintings and water colors, most of them of the modern Dutch school. The works formed the private stock of A Augustus Healy of Brooklyn. They were to go at public sale on Friday evening, February 15, at Mendelssohn Hall on Fortieth Street. Thomas Kirby of the association ran the sale.

The terms of sale are printed in full at the front. The highest bidder is the buyer, and a lot in dispute goes up again at once. Buyers must give their names and homes, pay a cash deposit down, and take their lots away within twenty-four hours. The house makes no pledge as to the truth of its accounts of the works. Such catalogues now record what Dutch art fetched at auction then.
70987-the-comic-history-of-the-united-st:
John Sherwood wrote The Comic History of the United States, published in Boston by Fields, Osgood in 1870, with original illustrations by Harry Scratchly. The subtitle gives the span: from a period prior to the discovery of America to times long subsequent to the present. A Horace motto heads the title page: what forbids telling the truth with a laugh?

The frontispiece is pun-named a Con-front-us Piece, showing the company of comedians engaged for the performance. An old song supplies the second motto: a man may say a wise thing though he say it with a laugh. Sherwood marches the national story from before Columbus onward, treating presidents and wars as a stage comedy. Readers of 1870 got their country's past as a burlesque with pictures.
71125-how-the-shortage-of-skilled-mechan:
How the Shortage of Skilled Mechanics Is Being Overcome by Training the Unskilled is a wartime pamphlet dated September 1918. It comes from the Section on Industrial Training for the War Emergency, under the Committee on Labor of the Council of National Defense. War work needed machinists faster than the trades could supply them, and the pamphlet reports the training answer.

A national committee stands behind the plan, in three companies. Labor sends Frank Duffy of the carpenters and joiners, Hugh Frayne of the American Federation of Labor, and others from the unions and the Federal Board of Vocational Education. Employers send Henry Leland of the Lincoln Motor Company, mill and bridge men, and Percy Straus of Macy's. Education and welfare men complete the board, with branch chairmen for New England and Pennsylvania named.
7123-home-vegetable-gardening-a-complete:
F F Rockwell writes Home Vegetable Gardening as a complete and practical guide to planting and care of all vegetables, fruits, and berries worth growing for home use. The author of Around the Year in the Garden and Gardening Indoors and Under Glass addresses two classes. Some garden as a hobby, while others, in days of high prices, find it a great help. Many in both classes have narrow experience and limited spare time.

The book serves as first aid to such gardeners, who want practical, efficient work with the least fuss and loss of time. Rockwell notes garden books seldom lack information, yet often fail to present it in the clearest way. His guide therefore orders each crop plainly, from planting to table, for the home gardener.
72144-survey-of-london-volume-05-of-14-t:
Volume five of the Survey of London gives the parish of Saint Giles in the Fields, part two. The London County Council issued the book in nineteen hundred fourteen. Sir Laurence Gomme and Philip Norman led the joint work. W Edward Riley drew the plans and gave the building notes.

The Survey aims to log each old part of greater London in full. A joint board of council and survey men ran the task. The Earl of Curzon of Kedleston led the survey group then. Drawings, plates, and close notes fill the parish record. Each house and site of note gets its own weighed tale. Spring Gardens, the council’s home, signs the title page here. Part one of the parish had filled an earlier volume. This half rounds the Saint Giles story for the shelf.
7321-the-nibelungenlied-translated-into-:
George Henry Needler, associate professor of German at University College, Toronto, translates the Nibelungenlied into rhymed English verse in the metre of the original. His preface states a simple purpose: to place one of the world's great epic poems within reach of English readers. Translations are at best poor substitutes for originals, he admits, and a new version implies a criticism of those before it.

Needler's apology rests on metre: no earlier English version, he argues, reproduced the original's metrical form, and his hope is to make the poem's outlines clear in its own music. The epic of Siegfried, Kriemhild, and Burgundian doom thus gains an English shape that honours its German verse. Scholars and general readers share the gain.
