It is made to pass the pupil from the easier ground of the Third to the harder course of the Union Fifth Reader. That Reader is next higher in the series. The book is carefully graded to that middle position.

In one sense, Sanders argues, the Fourth Reader is the most important in the set. The great mass of pupils in common schools are drawn away from school pursuits long before the proper time for a more advanced course. That fact weighed fully in preparing the pages.
snowflakes-and-sunbeams-or-the-young-fur: R. M. Ballantyne wrote The Young Fur-Traders, and the contents open in the middle of an Arctic winter in the wilds of North America. Heads bring in the old fur-trader, who tries to fix his son's flint and finds the task hard, then a counting-room scene. A wolf-hunt on the prairies follows, where Charley stuns his father and breaks in the new horse. Peter Mactavish turns amateur doctor, and Charley airs his views to Kate before the spring brigade sets out.
studies-in-the-psychology-of-sex-volume-:
Volume V of Havelock Ellis's Studies in the Psychology of Sex, dated 1927, holds Erotic Symbolism, The Mechanism of Detumescence, and The Psychic State in Pregnancy. Ellis calls these the terminal phenomena of the sexual process, treated before the final volume turns to morals and social hygiene.

Under erotic symbolism Ellis places nearly all the stray forms of the sexual instinct. In each, he argues, some object or act has gained a dynamic power over the mind and body: clear in shoe fetishism, dimmer in exhibitionism. Calling them sexual equivalents only labels them; symbolism, he claims, gives the key that makes them intelligible, whether their roots are inborn, acquired, or both.
ten-reasons-proposed-to-his-adversaries-:
Edmund Campion, a priest of the Society of Jesus, wrote Ten Reasons, his Decem Rationes, as a challenge to foes of the Catholic faith at the English universities. An opening essay in this printing traces the work's long life and high praise.

The essay notes forty-seven printings across Europe and a verdict by Mark Anthony Muret that it was written by the finger of God. It calls the work Campion's last free word on his brief English mission. He had checked the tide of the new faith when the old church seemed down for good. Readers get a famed piece of Elizabethan religious debate, framed by its martyr's fate.
the-abolition-of-slavery-the-right-of-th:
William Lloyd Garrison and others stand behind The Abolition of Slavery. Its full title claims the right of the government under the war power. The pieces argue that the federal war power can end slavery. A part on freedom under the war power opens the book.

That part quotes John Quincy Adams at length. Adams spoke in the House on April 14 and 15, 1842. The topic was war with Great Britain and Mexico. Adams grants that Congress may not meddle with slavery in the states. That holds while slave states keep to their own bounds. But the case changes once the topic is forced on the House. It changes once a member is censured unheard. Readers get a core legal case for wartime freedom. It was built from speeches made years before the Civil War.
the-authoritative-life-of-general-willia:
G. S. Railton, described as first commissioner to General Booth, wrote an authorised life of William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army. Booth was born on April 10, 1829, and died on August 20, 1912, the year this life was copyrighted. A preface by General Bramwell Booth opens the volume.

Twenty-eight chapters trace Booth from childhood and poverty through youth, lay work, and early ministry. Later chapters follow work in East London, the making of an army, and growth in America, Australasia, India, South Africa, and Japan. Final sections cover social work, finance, old age, tributes, organisation, and Booth as a writer.
the-circus-boys-on-the-flying-rings-or-m:
Edgar B. P. Darlington opens this boys' circus tale, subtitled Making the Start in the Sawdust Life, with two boys before a circus billboard. Teddy boasts that he can do what the pictured performer is doing in the air. Phil, his friend, laughs the claim down and corrects his terms.

That is no cartwheel, Phil tells him, but a double somersault, and a real stunt at that. The contents then follow Phil's path: he hears his dismissal, makes his start in the world, and proves his mettle when the circus comes to town. He makes friends with the elephants, enters the sawdust arena, and wins his first call and a thrilling rescue. Setbacks follow, including being left behind and a startling discovery. Darlington gives young readers a backstage path into circus work, from first longing to a solved mystery.
the-collected-works-of-ambrose-bierce-vo: Volume VIII of Ambrose Bierce's collected works gathers his Negligible Tales, On with the Dance, and his Epigrams, shown here in a Gordian Press reprint of 1966. The title page notes that the volume was originally published in 1911. Only the front matter is present here, including the publisher's imprint and Library of Congress card number.A title page and a contents list are all that stand here.
the-continental-monthly-vol-iii-issue-vi:
June 1863 brings the sixth number of volume III of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece is the second part of The Value of the Union. Having surveyed the Union's worth and growth in the first part, the writer now turns to face the pro-slavery rebellion and its drift.

The argument runs through sacred history: a kind Providence, the essay says, has always pushed mankind toward a higher, more united, and happier life, against the drag of selfishness and ignorance. Ages of political upheaval and such religious light as men could take in raised Europe to its state of two and a half centuries ago. There the seeds of religious and political liberty sprouted and crossed to the new world, where they grew into the republic.
the-divine-right-of-church-government-wh: The Divine Right of Church Government argues that rule by preaching and ruling elders alone can claim God's warrant from Scripture. The title page credits sundry ministers of Christ in London. It notes a new, corrected edition printed in New York in 1844. An added part draws on strong writers about church rule. Only the title pages are present here. Their lines cover who may preach, who may join a church, and the people's right to choose pastors.
the-golden-treasury-of-the-best-songs-an: Francis Turner Palgrave selected The Golden Treasury of the Best Songs and Lyrical Pieces in the English Language. Collins' Clear-Type Press printed it in London and Glasgow. Pictures are by A. Pearse. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and Palgrave's dedication to Alfred Tennyson, Poet Laureate. In it he says the book grew under Tennyson's advice. He had hoped to dedicate it to Henry Hallam, who died before it was done. He calls it a true national anthology of three centuries.
the-great-lone-land-a-narrative-of-trave:
Colonel W. F. Butler wrote The Great Lone Land. It is a narrative of travel and adventure in the North-West of America. Sampson Low, Marston and Company printed it in London. It was first published in 1872. The title page quotes Tennyson on a full-fed river and an endless plain. His preface tells of a man at York Factory on Hudson Bay. That man had one fixed resolution. It was to write a book.

The man used to say he would set down all he had seen, and all he had not seen. Butler doubts the plan. People, he says, more readily believe what a man has not seen. He tells of Karkakonias, a Chippeway chief taken to Washington during the Southern War. The aim was to astonish him with American power. He came home silent, and spent his days in smoking and quiet thought.
the-heavenly-footman-or-a-description-of:
John Bunyan wrote The Heavenly Footman, subtitled a description of the man that gets to heaven, with directions how to run so as to obtain. The title page carries the text from First Corinthians: so run, that ye may obtain. An author's letter addresses slothful and careless people at length.

Bunyan warns that sloth in the work of salvation fills the heart with sin, shuts out Christ, and shames the soul. He cites Solomon on the sluggard, the ant as a teacher, and the man who will not plow because of the cold. Neglect of the season for getting heaven, he argues, brings late and bitter repentance in its train.
the-history-of-tom-thumb-to-which-are-ad:
The History of Tom Thumb was edited by Henry Altemus. Two more stories are added to the title tale. They are The Cat and the Mouse and Fire! Fire! Burn Stick! The title story opens in the days of Prince Arthur, king of Britain in the year 516. Merlin, a great magician, travels in beggar's disguise.

Tired, Merlin stops at the cottage of an honest ploughman. The ploughman's wife serves milk and coarse brown bread. Sadness in the neat home leads Merlin to ask its cause. The pair long for a child, he learns. The wife would accept a son no bigger than a thumb. A sibling record tells the same tale with a different opening.
the-inns-and-taverns-of-pickwick-with-so: B. W. Matz wrote this guide to the inns of Dickens's Pickwick Papers, with observations on their other associations. Only the title page and contents are present here. The tour itself does not appear. The contents open with Pickwick and the coaching age. The Golden Cross at Charing Cross comes first. The Bull at Rochester and the White Hart in the Borough follow. Later stops include the Leather Bottle at Cobham, the Great White Horse at Ipswich, and the George and Vulture. A frontispiece shows Pickwick starting for Ipswich.
the-nibelungenlied-translated-into-rhyme:
George Henry Needler's translation of the Nibelungenlied renders the German epic into rhymed English verse in the metre of the original. Needler taught German as associate professor in University College, Toronto. He states his purpose plainly in a preface dated September 1904. He wanted to put a great epic poem, one of the world's finest, within reach of English readers.

Translations are poor substitutes, he concedes, and a new one implies criticism of its predecessors. His apology is that no earlier version reproduced the original's metrical form. His introduction supplies the historical background, summing up research into the saga's origin and growth. Needler had begun the translation years before, while studying the original under Zarncke at Leipzig. Contents outline the introduction's treatment of the saga in its northern and German forms.
the-nile-tributaries-of-abyssinia-and-th:
Only the Project Gutenberg header for The Nile Tributaries of Abyssinia is present here, so Samuel W. Baker's narrative itself does not appear. The header names Baker as author and dates the electronic text May 1999, number 2125 in the Gutenberg series. Nothing of Abyssinia, the Nile, or the sword hunters of the book's fuller title is included in these pages.

They explain that the texts are usually created from multiple editions, all in the public domain within the United States, and that no particular paper edition is kept exactly. Release dates, file naming, and a known fault in the project's file server that scrambles dates are discussed in the boilerplate.
the-north-pole-its-discovery-in-1909-und:
Robert E. Peary wrote the account of reaching the North Pole in 1909, first published in 1910. Theodore Roosevelt wrote the introduction, and Gilbert H. Grosvenor of the National Geographic Society wrote the foreword. The trip was made under the Peary Arctic Club. Peary dedicated the book to his wife.

An early picture shows five flags planted at the Pole, held by Peary's Inuit companions and Matthew Henson. The flags stand for the Navy League, a college fraternity, the D.A.R. peace cause, and the Red Cross, plus a polar flag Peary had carried for fifteen years. Readers get the commander's own record of the dash to the Pole.
the-outdoor-chums-after-big-game-or-peri: Captain Quincy Allen wrote The Outdoor Chums After Big Game, or Perilous Adventures in the Wilderness, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and a list of the series are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The frontispiece caption shows a beast filled with mad rage galloping straight toward the boys. The series list names companion volumes on the lake, in the forest, and on the Gulf, each at 50 cents postpaid.
the-pony-rider-boys-in-new-mexico-or-the:
Frank Gee Patchin's The Pony Rider Boys in New Mexico, or The End of the Silver Trail, dated 1910, opens aboard an Atlantic and Pacific train. Two men talk in low voices a few seats ahead of four sleeping boys, taking care not to be understood. One has heard of the boys over in Nevada. There are four of them, the Pony Rider Boys, and no tenderfeet, if the stories of their stunts are true.

The talk turns to the stock car up ahead, jammed with stock and equipment. It turns to one slick roan pony a man would not mind owning, by trade or otherwise. A loud snore from Stacy Brown makes both men laugh. Tad Butler rests beside him, and Ned Rector and the fourth boy sleep further back. Patchin lets the reader hear the plotting first, so the danger hangs over the holiday from the opening pages.
the-poor-scholar-traits-and-stories-of-t:
William Carleton's The Poor Scholar stands as Part VI of his Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry. One day about the middle of November, Dominick M'Evoy and his son Jemmy are at work on their potatoes. Their plot lies on Esker Dhu, a hard and barren hill. The day is bitter, the men thinly clad. Sleet-like rain pelts into their garments as the blast sweeps across the hill.

The father, past middle age, holds his miserable farm at a rack-rent and must work it whatever the weather. Pausing on his spade, he looks down at the sheltered inland below. It is inhabited chiefly by Protestants and Presbyterians. He nearly curses them for sitting warm in his people's old possessions. The two ridges before him hold only a poor string of potatoes, one here and one there. Yet the whole ridge must be turned for them.
the-positive-school-of-criminology-three:
Enrico Ferri's The Positive School of Criminology collects three lectures given at the University of Naples on April 22, 23, and 24, 1901. Ernest Untermann translated them, and Charles H. Kerr and Company published them at Chicago in 1908. Untermann's name is printed on this record's own title page. Several hundred students had invited Ferri to sum up the principal conclusions of criminal sociology in short special lectures. He says he gladly accepted.

Two ideals moved him. The first was personal: to spread the scientific ideas his brain had gathered, a prize he credits to his mother's inheritance in the lottery of life. The second was the ideal of young Italy, united in moral and intellectual aims and lifted above the grasp of selfish interests. Without an ideal, Ferri tells his audience, neither an individual nor a whole people can live. It is the fire that makes each life possible, useful, and fertile.
the-power-of-faith-exemplified-in-the-li: The Power of Faith presents the life and writings of the late Mrs. Isabella Graham in a new edition from the American Tract Society. Joanna Bethune entered the copyright in 1843. The edition is enriched by Graham's own narrative of her husband's death and other select correspondence. What appears here is the title page and the start of a detailed contents list. Chapter I covers her early life and residence in Canada, from birth and conversion through marriage to a voyage to Quebec, Montreal, and Antigua, across 1742 to 1772.
the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-in-nine: Volume three of Johnson's works in the nine-volume 1825 edition is shown through title pages and a contents list. A clash stands on those pages: the volume is the third of the set, yet its heading names The Rambler, volume two, and the contents list covers that second Rambler volume. Listed essays run from number 106 to 118. Topics include authors' expectations, prostitutes' misery, and Hymenaeus's courtship. The essays themselves do not appear in the pages present.

Volume four of Johnson's works, in the nine-volume 1825 edition, pairs The Adventurer with The Idler. A prefatory notice explains how The Adventurer began. Dr. John Hawkesworth projected the paper in 1752, admiring The Rambler. Its first number appeared on November 7 that year. Size, price, and publication days matched The Rambler's pattern.

Johnson joined the writers in 1753. His first paper is dated March 3. He then recruited his friend Dr. Joseph Warton to help. Dr. Bathurst, Colman, and Mrs. Chapone also contributed. The notice sets up Johnson's share in a famous periodical. Readers learn how essay papers were planned, staffed, and sustained.
thoughts-i-met-on-the-highway-words-of-f: Ralph Waldo Trine published Thoughts I Met on the Highway with Dodd, Mead in New York in 1919, copyrighted in 1912. The subtitle promises words of friendly cheer from his Life Books. Other Trine titles listed include In Tune with the Infinite and The Land of Living Men. A first line begins by calling thoughts forces that build and attract their like, then breaks off. The title pages and book lists are what is included in this record, so Trine's reflections themselves do not appear beyond that opening line.
timothy-s-quest-a-story-for-anybody-youn: Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote Timothy's Quest, subtitled a story for anybody, young or old, who cares to read it. Houghton, Mifflin published it at Boston and New York, printed at the Riverside Press in Cambridge. A publisher's list prices her Birds' Christmas Carol and Story of Patsy alongside it. Wiggin is also credited with A Summer in a Canon, Children's Rights, and Polly Oliver's Problem in that list. The publisher's catalogue and title page are what is on these pages, so Wiggin's story itself does not appear.
un-doc-agreement-relating-to-the-impleme:
The Agreement on the Implementation of Part XI of the Law of the Sea Convention was signed at New York on 28 July 1994. Part XI governs mining of the deep seabed beyond any state's waters. Rich states had shunned the 1982 pact over those rules. Talks from 1990 to 1994 sought a fix all could accept.

The deal reads Part XI through a market lens. Where the two texts clash, this one wins. Joining the sea pact after 1994 counts as joining this deal too. The deep seabed and its wealth stay the shared birthright of all mankind. The change cleared the way for near-universal buy-in to the sea rules.
un-un-res-agreement-relating-to-the-impl:
Deep seabed mining rules in the Law of the Sea Convention were rewritten by this agreement, adopted by the United Nations in 1994. Part XI of the 1982 convention had set up a strict shared system for mining the ocean floor. Rich states refused to join while those rules stood, and the whole treaty stalled.

The agreement softens the mining rules, cuts costs, and gives market states more say. In exchange, the rest of the convention could enter into force at last. The text is a case study in how a grand treaty gets saved by a practical rewrite.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: A Project Gutenberg header is all that is present here, and Widger's quotations from William Dean Howells are not shown. The header marks the set DW number 04 in the Quotations series by David Widger. It uses the older Gutenberg welcome form, with a state-by-state donation list from about 2000. Readers are told to check the copyright laws of their own country before sharing the file. No title block with release date appears in the portion shown here.
women-in-the-fine-arts-from-the-seventh-: Clara Erskine Clement surveyed women artists from the seventh century B. C. to the twentieth century in this 1904 volume. Pages present here hold her prefatory note and a list of illustrations, but no artist entries. Clement explains that she wrote to artists in Britain, Europe, and America asking about training, honours, and main works. Many sent photographs of their art for the plates. The frontispiece shows Elisabetta Sirani's Infant Christ in Bologna.
wonders-of-creation-a-descriptive-accoun:
Published in 1872 for young readers, this volume describes volcanoes and what they do. Its preface says plain treatment comes first. Hard science and deep theory are left aside on purpose. The hope is that early wonder will push some readers toward later study. A holiday trip to Vesuvius or Etna now sits within reach, the preface notes.

Hecla and its geysers, Cotopaxi, and Kilauea all get named as future goals. The preface also frames volcanoes as proof of divine power and wise limits. Young readers learn basic facts about eruptions, craters, and lava. A sense of awe runs through the lessons.
yorkshire-lyrics-poems-written-in-the-di: John Hartley wrote these lyrics in the dialect spoken in Yorkshire's West Riding. He dedicated the gathering to his daughter Annie Sophie at Christmas 1898. Pages present here hold the title page, that dedication, and a contents list. Titles include Mi Bonny Yorksher Lass, A Tale for th' Childer on Christmas Eve, and Words ov Kindness. A selection of plainer fugitive verses was added, per the title page. The poems themselves do not appear in these pages.
